summary:
Utah regulates where transgender people may use restrooms and locker rooms. HB 257, signed by Governor Spencer Cox on 30 January 2024, requires people to use bathrooms and locker rooms in public schools and government-owned buildings according to sex assigned at birth. The law does not apply to private businesses. A person challenged under the statute may defend themselves by presenting documentation: a birth certificate, and, where the marker has been changed, proof of gender-affirming surgery. New government buildings must include single-occupant bathrooms. By the time of signing, at least 10 other states had enacted comparable bathroom-regulation laws.

Utah operates a reporting mechanism under HB 257. A state form allows residents to report transgender people using 'privacy spaces' such as changing rooms and restrooms; complainants may choose whether their names are included while the state investigates each reported violation. A May 2024 procedure permits officials and individuals to file formal complaints about suspected incorrect bathroom use in schools and government buildings. The ACLU of Utah opposed the bill on the ground that it risks discriminatory enforcement.

Utah restricts transgender students' housing. In 2024 the state passed a bill banning transgender students from dorms aligned with their gender identity, following an incident in which a transgender woman was assigned to a girls' dorm at Utah State University.

Utah bans gender-affirming care for minors. Legislation passed by the House on 26 January 2023 and the Senate 20-8 on 27 January was signed on 28 January 2023 with immediate effect. Continuation of care was permitted only for youth already receiving it in January 2023. Doctors may provide such care to persons aged 18 to 24, but those patients retain a retroactive right to disaffirm consent and sue. A legislative legal review found the ban potentially unconstitutional for targeting transgender people. A two-year systematic review released in May 2025, commissioned under the ban, concluded that the treatments are effective for mental health and psychosocial outcomes and for body changes consistent with affirmed gender, and safe regarding bone density, cardiovascular risk, metabolic changes and cancer; the legislature dismissed the findings and kept the ban in place.

Utah restricts transgender athletes' participation in sport. House Bill 11, banning transgender athletes from sports, athletics and the Olympics, passed in March 2022 and was vetoed by Governor Spencer Cox on 22 March 2022; the Legislature overrode the veto to take effect 1 July, and a judge partly reversed it on 19 August, allowing transgender girls to be considered case-by-case for girls' sports in 2022-2023. On 3 October 2024, Southern Utah University and Utah State University forfeited matches against San Jose State University amid litigation over a transgender player under NCAA sport-by-sport eligibility and testosterone standards.

Utah restricts display of LGBTQ+ flags. On 7 May 2025 the state became the first to explicitly prohibit flying LGBTQ+ flags at government buildings and schools, with fines of $500 a day; a March 2025 law had already banned LGBTQ pride flags on public schools and government buildings. Utah Pride's executive director said the state 'leads the nation in anti-LGBTQ legislation.' In May 2025 Salt Lake City adopted the Sego Visibility Flag, based on the transgender pride flag, as an official city flag.

Identity documents in Utah are comparatively open. Transgender people may amend the gender marker on a birth certificate by submitting a certified court order changing name and gender, without requiring sex reassignment surgery; an 'X' descriptor is available subject to judicial approval. In May 2021 the Utah Supreme Court held 4-1 that judges must grant such sex and name changes when clinical requirements are met.

Utah provides statutory non-discrimination and hate-crime protection with gaps. SB 296, passed by the Senate 23-5 on 6 March 2015, approved by the House 65-10 on 11 March and signed 12 March 2015, bans discrimination based on gender identity in employment and housing but not public accommodations, and exempts religious organizations and affiliates including schools and hospitals. The hate-crime statute amended in 2019 (Senate 18-11 on 5 March, House 64-9 on 12 March, Senate concurrence 22-3, signed 2 April) criminalizes hate crimes based on gender identity and requires collection and publication of hate-crime statistics.

Utah prohibits conversion therapy on minors. The prohibition was established by Governor Gary Herbert's executive order of 21 January 2020 and codified by legislation passed in February 2023 covering LGBT minors, while exempting clergy, religious counselors, parents and grandparents unless acting as psychologists.

In March 2024 a U.S. Department of Justice investigation found that the Utah Department of Corrections discriminated against an inmate by denying gender-affirming hormones.
tangentialFactors:
Utah's flag ban places it ahead of comparable measures elsewhere: similar flag bans were signed in Idaho and Montana, while Salt Lake City issued counter-flags and Boise made the pride flag an official city flag. Utah's bathroom law was among at least 10 state bathroom-regulation statutes in force by January 2024.

The state's care ban sits within a wider national pattern of restrictions on gender-affirming care for minors, and Utah's own legislative legal review flagged the ban as potentially unconstitutional for singling out transgender people.

The 2024 dormitory restriction and the HB 257 reporting form both arose from or follow individual incidents and complaint procedures rather than broad enforcement campaigns; the available sources do not document how many complaints the form has received or how they were resolved.
